bib.title: IPython: Beyond Normal Python (Chapter 1, Python Data Science Handbook)
bib.venue: O'Reilly (book chapter; no copyright page in the PDF, edition and year not printed; text shows IPython 4.0.1 and mentions the 2016 Windows Bash announcement, so 2016 first edition is inferred)

question: Which IPython shell and notebook features (help, tab completion, magics, history, shell access, debugging, profiling) make interactive data science work faster?
contributions: Tour of IPython help (?, ??, Tab, wildcards), shell shortcuts, magic commands, In/Out history, shell integration, %xmode/%debug, and timing/profiling magics

results.claim: %timeit shows a list comprehension is about 10% faster than the equivalent for loop for squares of range(1000).
results.setup: %timeit on L = [n ** 2 for n in range(1000)]; for-loop version %%timeit gave 373 µs. IPython 4.0.1 era (Python 2/3 transitional), author's laptop, hardware unstated
results.quote: 1000 loops, best of 3: 325 µs per loop

results.claim: The for-loop version of the same computation takes 373 µs per loop.
results.setup: %%timeit with L.append(n ** 2) loop, range(1000). IPython 4.0.1 era (Python 2/3 transitional), author's laptop, hardware unstated
results.quote: 1000 loops, best of 3: 373 µs per loop

results.claim: Sorting an unsorted list of 100000 floats takes 41.5 ms wall time under %time.
results.setup: %time L.sort() on 100000 random floats, single run. IPython 4.0.1 era (Python 2/3 transitional), author's laptop, hardware unstated

results.claim: Sorting an already sorted list takes 8.24 ms wall time under %time; repeated %timeit on L.sort() is misleading because later runs sort sorted data.
results.setup: %time L.sort() again on the same, now sorted, list. IPython 4.0.1 era (Python 2/3 transitional), author's laptop, hardware unstated

results.claim: %timeit on L.sort() reports 1.9 ms per loop, skewed by repeated sorting of presorted data.
results.setup: %timeit L.sort() on 100000 random floats. IPython 4.0.1 era (Python 2/3 transitional), author's laptop, hardware unstated
results.quote: 100 loops, best of 3: 1.9 ms per loop

results.claim: %prun on sum_of_lists(1000000) shows 14 function calls in 0.714 seconds, with 0.599 s in the list comprehension.
results.setup: %prun sum_of_lists(1000000). IPython 4.0.1 era (Python 2/3 transitional), author's laptop, hardware unstated

results.claim: %lprun attributes 95.9% of time to the list-comprehension line of sum_of_lists(5000).
results.setup: %lprun -f sum_of_lists sum_of_lists(5000); line 4, 9001 us of 9382 us total. IPython 4.0.1 era (Python 2/3 transitional), author's laptop, hardware unstated; quote is the line label, value from table row 4

results.claim: %memit reports peak memory 100.08 MiB for sum_of_lists(1000000).
results.setup: %memit sum_of_lists(1000000) with memory_profiler. IPython 4.0.1 era (Python 2/3 transitional), author's laptop, hardware unstated

results.claim: %mprun shows creating the list L adds about 25 MB (25.4 MiB) of memory.
results.setup: %mprun on mprun_demo.sum_of_lists(1000000), line 4. IPython 4.0.1 era (Python 2/3 transitional), author's laptop, hardware unstated
results.quote: 71.9 MiB     25.4 MiB           L = [j ^ (j >> i) for j in range(N)]

results.claim: The shell offers 399 importable modules for tab completion on the author's system (system dependent).
results.setup: import <TAB> on the author's machine. Varies per install.

limits: Version-dated: IPython 4.0.1 and Jupyter notebook of 2015-2016; Python 2/3 transitional era. Timing outputs use 'best of 3' and 'loops' wording; modern %timeit prints 'mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs'.
Timing numbers come from one unspecified machine and are illustrative, not benchmarks.
%mprun works only for functions defined in separate modules, not the notebook itself (p.29).
Windows shell commands may fail; text says native Bash on Windows may fix this 'soon'.
The 'jupyter notebook' launch and NotebookApp log lines are dated; current tooling is Jupyter Lab/Notebook 7.
Shell shortcuts depend on GNU Readline and may differ by system.
practices: Use ? for docs, ?? for source, and Tab for exploration; add docstrings to your own code (p.3-5).
Use wildcard matching with * to find names (e.g. str.*find*?) (p.7-8).
Use %paste/%cpaste to paste code with prompt markers (p.11).
Use %run to run scripts inside the session; their functions remain defined (p.12).
Use %timeit for short statements and %time when repetition would skew the result, e.g. sorting (p.26).
Use semicolon to suppress output and avoid storing it in Out (p.15).
Use %debug after an exception, %pdb on to auto-launch, and %xmode Plain/Context/Verbose to control traceback detail (p.21-23).
Profile in order: %timeit, %prun, %lprun, then %memit/%mprun; do not optimise early (Knuth quote, p.25).
Use %cd, not !cd, to change directory, because ! runs in a temporary subshell (p.19).

terms.definition: denoted by a single % prefix and operate on a single line of input
denoted by a double %% prefix and operate on multiple lines of input
magic functions such as cd, ls, cp usable without the % sign, toggled with %automagic
IPython.utils.text.SList, list-like shell return type with grep and fields methods and s, n, p properties
In is a list of past inputs (index 0 is a placeholder); Out is a dict mapping input numbers to outputs; _, __, ___ and _N are shortcuts
